utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can I have the interpreter's voice louder, please? I can't hear them very well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: The Chamber is of the view that in view of that answer, the suggestion of a need for consideration of documents overnight is unnecessary. The issue of the decision, we think in view of the hour and the reference that's been made to authority, that we ought to give our decision on resumption tomorrow. There is the question of the one document, the card. Are you proposing that it should be tendered at this point, Mr. Whiting, or not?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Yeah, I think that's fine that it be tendered.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Well, we'll at least accomplish something at this point. Is there any concern about the receipt of that KLA card upon which the witness placed some reliance?

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. Your Honour, would you just permit me to have a word with Mr. Mansfield a moment before raise for the day?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Perhaps while that's happening, if you would be kind enough, would you give to the court officer again the KLA card that you had, sir? It will be -- is this a document that is of personal significance to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, because this is a document that shows when Ruzhdi Selihu's battalion was formed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Are you -- would you prefer to take this document back with you for your personal purposes?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I would like that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Would counsel be content if a copy was made of the document and the copy received as an exhibit?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Most definitely.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Certainly, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes. We'll make a copy of this document overnight and tomorrow return the original to you so that you have it for your personal records in the future.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The exhibit number will be P117.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, Mr. Topolski, is there anything coming from that discussion?

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Well, I think Mr. Mansfield is going to raise a matter that I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: -- was going to raise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Mansfield.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: Yes. Your Honours, I don't know whether in fact in the morning -- I'm so sorry, in the afternoon tomorrow we might have an opportunity just to add some observations about Mr. Whiting's submissions this afternoon; if not, I would obviously do them now. But in addition to that, plainly there are more documents. There are notes that he has mentioned that he has at home. Now, I don't know whether they're the same notes or different notes, but he does mention notes in his interview that has been referred to; it's on page 77. Now, whether these are part of the same set of notes he was keeping - it refers to a particular part of 1998 - I don't know. But in any event, it's clear he does have notes. And so we say the matter isn't entirely closed as far as that's concerned because the point that I would have made at this stage - I'll put it shortly so as not to take up too much time with it at the moment - is that of course our major contention is there has been no change. Mr. Whiting has said many --

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Excuse me. I'm sorry. But could we excuse the witness again if we're going to take up this matter?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We're going to have to continue our deliberations of the point of difficulty so that -- I think given the hour, the most practical course would be for you to be excused tonight, for your evidence to continue tomorrow when we resume at 2.15 in the afternoon. So if you would be good enough to go with the court officer now and you'll be given detailed assistance with the time and et cetera for your return tomorrow to continue your evidence. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'd --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Were you in midstream, Mr. Mansfield?

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: Yes, I was slightly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Midstream.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Could we go into private session.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: Yes, all right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Tuesday, the 1st day of February, 2005, at 2.15 p.m.
